#53180. Zoning reform is remaking parking lots into a housing paradise

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1325 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Zoning reform is remaking parking lots into a housing paradise

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Developers across the country paved over paradise to put up a parking lot.
  • It has been revealed that in California, a series of state laws has made that easier.
  • According to recent reports, much of the zoning reform push across the country focuses on where ground-up developers could build residential density, particularly infill in urban areas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Developers across the country paved over paradise to put up a parking lot. But changes to zoning laws to increase housing supply now have developers paving over parking lots to create a housing paradise.

It has been revealed that in California, a series of state laws has made that easier. Florida lawmakers have gone after the same land. San Diego suburb National City took matters into its own hands. Because of its high housing costs, California has been the leading model for how reforms can work. But the Golden State is also a model for how neighborhood advocates and cities fight the reforms, often rendering them worth less than the paper they’re written on.

According to recent reports, much of the zoning reform push across the country focuses on where ground-up developers could build residential density, particularly infill in urban areas. The pressure is on land.

According to recent reports, underused parking lots are one option. The median share of downtown land used only for parking is about 26% in U.S. cities with more than 500,000 people, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation.

California’s Assembly Bill 2011 created a ministerial approval path, exempt from environmental review, for apartments on sites where office, retail or parking is a principal use. AB 2243 expanded those tools for commercially zoned property when it took effect last year.

Florida’s Live Local Act requires cities and counties to allow multifamily rentals by right on commercial, industrial and mixed-use land when a share of the units is affordable. Lawmakers have amended the law multiple times, including this year, since enactment in 2023.

According to recent reports, national City reveals how the local action can work. The city loosened height limits in its mixed-use zones last year, making underused lots more workable for housing.

It has been revealed that national City Investment Group has broken ground on Market View, a 120-unit workforce housing project that will replace a parking lot beside Manolo Farmers Market in National City. This small grocery chain has locations in San Diego, where leaders have instituted reforms that have faced neighborhood challenges and lawsuits that new state law quashes.

Opponents still turn to the courts, even though reforms were meant to curtail or preclude lawsuits. And they are getting more inventive.

In San Francisco, neighbors are suing over an 848-unit project at 15 Marina Blvd. The towers would replace the Safeway’s parking lot and rise above a newly built store. They say the city wrongly ruled it eligible for AB 2011 and denied them a hearing.

To get the case into federal court, local opponents invoked an 1871 law, commonly known as the Ku Klux Klan Act. The developer wants the federal court to dismiss the case.

Recent findings suggest that in Los Angeles, the fight is over habitat. Planners rejected 398 homes at the Woodland Hills Country Club in August, citing mountain lions. The state Department of Housing and Community Development remarked the city violated AB 2011. Pro-housing groups have sued the city while the developer threatens its own lawsuit for damages that could exceed $20 million.

According to recent reports, under AB 2011, a qualifying project gets ministerial approval, which means municipal staff checks it against objective standards and no hearing is required. Residents lose the chance to comment on the project or its environmental effects, said Sheri Bonstelle, a land-use attorney at Greenberg Lusker who represents developers, told HousingWire TBD.

“Neighbors are really upset that they no longer have a voice at all,” Bonstelle mentioned.

Developers will also pay for the faster path. AB 2011 projects must meet labor standards, including prevailing wage. Bonstelle said that can add roughly 30% to construction costs, which developers weigh against discretionary review and the risk of a lawsuit under the California Environmental Quality Act.

“It’s literally a monetary analysis,” Bonstelle noted.

The math has worked for some of her clients, she remarked. They’ll trade off higher costs for the elimination of entitlement risk and confidence that a project can be built. Bonstelle said lenders also favor the ministerial path. That’s especially crucial now, given the tight lending environment.

How much access neighbors get depends on the city. Los Angeles has a detailed AB 2011 application, Bonstelle said, so developers must file substantial information that neighbors can request and review. The city knew these projects were coming and was thorough about what had to be filed. Smaller cities are the bigger problem, she said.

“It’s more of an glitch with the smaller cities that haven’t had the projects come through yet,” Bonstelle remarked.

In a recent development, some cities hand developers a checklist meant for a building permit, she mentioned. Her firm then goes through item by item with city attorneys to explain that most of those materials are not due at the planning stage of ministerial review.

Other cities believe state law should not apply to them and decline to process applications, Bonstelle remarked. In one case, her firm is working with a small city that has been “incredibly difficult.” The firm is asking the state Department of Housing and Community Development for a technical assistance letter explaining what the law requires.

It has been revealed that florida’s Live Local Act addresses similar commercial land. Cities and counties must approve multifamily rentals administratively on commercial, industrial and mixed-use land, with no rezoning or public hearing, if at least 40% of units are affordable for 30 years. Lawmakers have amended the law three times since 2023, most recently in 2026.

According to recent reports, the law covers parking lots zoned for those uses, Patrick Chopson, an Atlanta architect and co-founder of Cove, told HousingWire TBD. “That’s a substantial deal,” Chopson remarked. Cove, which has a proprietary AI platform, recently acquired Deerfield Beach, Fla., architectural firm Gallo Herbert Architects. The firm has done a lot of work statewide in affordable housing.

It has been revealed that the act also funds projects. In St. Petersburg, Nashville-based Elmington Capital Group intends Skyway Flats, a 174-unit affordable apartment building on surface parking next to an assisted living facility in the city’s Skyway Marina District.

Industry observers note that the five-story building will have 28 one-bedroom, 100 two-bedroom and 46 three-bedroom apartments. All will target households earning 30% to 80% of the area median income, and 18 will go to young adults aging out of foster care.

Pinellas County commissioners unanimously approved $6 million in March to buy the land. The county will require affordability for 99 years. The $77 million project also draws on federal tax credit equity, tax-exempt bonds and a state loan through the Live Local Act.

Skyway Flats is in predevelopment. Elmington expects financial closing and a construction start in early 2027.

Similar to Pinellas County officials, National City planners acted on their own. They changed zoning to allow more density on parking lots. The change fits within the California law context. San Diego County alone needs more than 171,000 homes, regional officials say.

It has been revealed that the city’s planning commission began reforming the code in July 2025 to allow four stories. Previously, the code capped buildings at three.

That cap limited how many units a project could hold, Andrew Regenberg of Gafcon, the firm working with the owner, told the commission in a public hearing. Chris Dallo, who heads the investment group, backed the change.

“We believe that more housing means more opportunity not just for our market, but for local businesses,” Dallo told the commission.

Market View is scheduled for completion in the first quarter of 2028. It will have three buildings, mostly studios, one-bedrooms and two-bedrooms, linked by open space and the market. RDC designed it, and R.D. Olson Construction is the general contractor.

Councilmember Ditas Yamane, who represents the district, said the groundbreaking followed a long review.

“This milestone is the result of a long, thoughtful process and extensive due diligence to bring this vision to life,” Yamane said.

Coinbase announced its ChatGPT integration yesterday, allowing users to connect accounts and manage portfolios. Users can check balances, analyze holdings, and place eligible trades using everyday language. And every order requires explicit approval before execution.

The timing coincides with Pancake’s attempt to reposition itself beyond its original decentralized exchange business.

Before execution, ChatGPT displays an interactive confirmation card showing order details. Consumers must approve the transaction before Coinbase processes it through its Advanced Trade platform. Standard trading fees, eligibility requirements, and account limits still apply.

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong described the integration as another step toward an emerging agentic economy. The idea involves AI assistants handling increasingly complex financial tasks for users. But Coinbase still keeps humans responsible for approving individual trades for now.

While Coinbase expands through ChatGPT, Pancake is changing how owners perceive its decentralized trading ecosystem. Formerly known as PancakeSwap, the platform unveiled its rebrand today. The new identity reflects six years of expansion beyond its original token-swapping business.

Recent findings suggest that pancake now operates across more than 11 blockchain networks. The platform reports over 208 million users and more than $4.4 trillion in cumulative trading volume.

Sources indicate that its services now include perpetual contracts, tokenized stocks, ETFs, yield products, and developer infrastructure. The project is also preparing a dedicated mobile application. Its CAKE ticker and contract address remain unchanged, with existing staking positions unaffected.

Pancake’s relationship with Binance makes this rebrand interesting. Binance Labs announced a strategic investment in CAKE in June 2022. The investment supported the decentralized exchange’s development within the BNB Chain ecosystem.

The rivalry becomes clearer when looking beyond the latest announcements. Binance has already introduced its own AI infrastructure through Binance Agent OS. Launched in August 2026, the platform connects compatible AI applications with Binance trading, market data, wallet, and payment capabilities.

Sources indicate that its Model Context Protocol server supports compatible AI agents, including ChatGPT. Developers can build applications that access supported Binance services through user-controlled permissions.

Pancake is also developing its position in this emerging market. In July, the platform partnered with BNB Chain’s Agent Studio to help developers deploy autonomous agents.

Recent findings suggest that these agents can interact with Pancake’s liquidity pools, rebalance positions, and execute trading strategies. Its AI tools also include portfolio planning and assistance across DeFi products.

This creates an interesting contrast between the two ecosystems. Coinbase is bringing AI-powered trading directly to consumers through ChatGPT. Binance is building infrastructure that allows developers and AI agents to interact with its services. Pancake adds a decentralized execution layer to the wider BNB Chain ecosystem.

The next battle in crypto may not be about which exchange attracts the most human traders. It could be about which infrastructure becomes the preferred destination for AI-powered financial activity.

#53176. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no.
  • When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Sources indicate that expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

It has been revealed that A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

In a recent development, imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

Sources indicate that one of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

In a recent development, maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

Sources indicate that this is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Recent findings suggest that listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

Industry observers note that so, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

According to recent reports, “I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

Industry observers note that twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

According to recent reports, find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

In a recent development, we’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Boltz PBC, a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for pharmaceutical researchers, has raised $110 million in funding.
  • Bessemer led the Series A investment.
  • Small molecules, the building blocks of many drugs, can only neutralize a pathogen after binding to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:17 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Boltz PBC, a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for pharmaceutical researchers, has raised $110 million in funding.

Bessemer led the Series A investment. Boltz stated on Wednesday that the fund was joined by a large group of new and returning backers. The consortium included Greycroft, Andreessen Horowitz, Amplify Partners, F-Prime Capital, Hummingbird and others.

Small molecules, the building blocks of many drugs, can only neutralize a pathogen after binding to it. As a result, researchers start drug discovery projects by looking for molecules that have a high binding affinity with pathogens. They often review hundreds of thousands of candidate molecules per project. The process can take months and often costs millions of dollars.

Boltz offers an AI model called BoltzMol-1 that speeds up the workflow. It generates binding affinity data by reviewing only a few dozen, particularly promising molecules instead of the hundreds of thousands usually needed. The fewer molecules need to be studied, the less time the analysis takes.

It has been revealed that binding affinity evaluations don’t yield drug discoveries right away. Instead, they produce data points called small molecule hits. Those are essentially faint clues that help researchers pinpoint the area where they should focus their efforts.

Boltz staffers asked BoltzMol-1 to look for small molecule hits across 10 “challenging and therapeutically-relevant targets.” Targets are biological building blocks that play a role in disease processes. According to the tech giant, the model found small molecule hits for six of the targets.

Sources indicate that scientists can adapt BoltzMol-1 to project-specific constraints. If a research team has access to a relatively limited number of compounds, it could configure the model to only consider small molecules that can be made from those compounds. When material procurement is not an obstacle, BoltzMol-1 evaluates a much larger number of candidates.

Recent findings suggest that the firm also offers a second model called BoltzProt-1. It can generate tens of thousands of protein designs based on data gleaned from small molecule hits. Additionally, BoltzProt-1 automatically reviews each protein to determine if it could be used to develop a new drug.

Industry observers note that usually, AI models evaluate protein designs based on rubrics that provide only an indirect view of their effectiveness. BoltzProt-1 uses more direct metrics. The company states that BoltzProt-1’s protein evaluation mechanism demonstrated “higher success” than several competing models during internal tests.

Boltz sells its algorithms via an application programming interface that is billed based on token usage. According to the company, customers’ token consumption has grown by a factor of 50 since BoltzMol-1 and BoltzProt-1 introduced in June. Boltz counts six of the world’s 20 largest pharmaceutical companies as clients.

Industry observers note that the organization will use its upcoming funding to grow its headcount and procure more computing infrastructure. The extra hardware should make it easier for Boltz to keep up with leading AI labs such as newly public Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group. Over the past year, both companies have introduced models that are highly adapted to biology research tasks.

Boltz has already started training a upcoming generation of molecule design algorithms. The company says that they are “showing substantial improvements” over its current models.

Although the bank did not disclose the specific amount it had invested in the asset, the filing has triggered discussions as it highlights XRP’s growing exposure among institutional investors.

Unlike regular investors who purchase XRP directly from exchanges and hold in their wallets, the bank invested in XRP through Bitwise's fund.

With its XRP ETF offering, Bitwise allows traditional investors to gain exposure to XRP without having to manage the crypto asset themselves.

Although XRP has continued to see major institutions and banks join its ETF ecosystem, participation in the XRP funds have slowed significantly following the ongoing market volatility.

While the exposure showcased by the major Canadian bank shows growing XRP ETF adoption, it doesn’t change the fact that institutional traders are beginning to take caution as they have just recorded the highest weekly withdrawals since March 2026.

Mortgage delinquencies rise to 4.42% in Q3 2026

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mortgage delinquencies increased in the third quarter of 2026, with the share of loans at least one payment past due rising to 4.42%.
  • The seasonally adjusted delinquency rate for one- to four-unit residential properties was up 5 basis points from the second quarter and 43 bps from a year earlier.
  • In a recent development, foreclosure starts also increased, with the share of loans entering the foreclosure process rising 1 basis point from the previous quarter to 0.21%.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mortgage delinquencies increased in the third quarter of 2026, with the share of loans at least one payment past due rising to 4.42%. That’s according to the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA)’s National Delinquency Survey, released Thursday.

The seasonally adjusted delinquency rate for one- to four-unit residential properties was up 5 basis points from the second quarter and 43 bps from a year earlier.

In a recent development, foreclosure starts also increased, with the share of loans entering the foreclosure process rising 1 basis point from the previous quarter to 0.21%. The percentage of loans already in foreclosure reached 0.71%, up 4 bps quarterly and 21 bps year over year.

“Loans 90 days or more late or in foreclosure increased for the fifth consecutive quarter and are 51 basis points higher than the third quarter of 2025,” stated Marina Walsh, MBA’s vice president and head of industry analysis.

Recent findings suggest that walsh remarked the deterioration in government-backed loans is contributing to higher foreclosure activity. The Federal Housing Administration (FHA) foreclosure rate reached 1.89%, its highest level since the first quarter of 2017, while the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) foreclosure rate climbed to 1.06%, its highest since Q4 2016.

It has been revealed that by delinquency stage, the 30-day rate increased 4 basis points from the previous quarter to 2.25%, while the 60-day rate rose 1 bps to 0.74%. The 90-day delinquency rate remained unchanged at 1.43%.

Performance varied by loan type. The conventional mortgage delinquency rate increased by 1 basis point from the second quarter to 2.73%, while the FHA rate declined 5 bps to 11.74%. The VA delinquency rate rose 11 bps to 5%.

In a recent development, all three loan categories posted annual increases. Conventional delinquencies were up 11 bps from a year earlier, while FHA delinquencies increased 96 bps and VA delinquencies rose 50 bps.

The seriously delinquent rate, which includes loans at least 90 days past due or in the foreclosure process, reached 2.12% on a nonseasonally adjusted basis. That was up 6 basis points from the second quarter and 51 bps year over year.

FHA loans recorded the largest annual deterioration in serious delinquencies, with the rate rising 197 basis points. The rate increased 13 basis points for conventional loans and 60 basis points for VA loans.

In a recent development, the five states with the largest quarterly increases in overall mortgage delinquencies were Wyoming, up 72 basis points, followed by West Virginia and Louisiana, both up 32 basis points. Arkansas saw its rate increase by 31 basis points, while Kentucky’s rose by 27 bps.

Walsh mentioned the overall mortgage delinquency rate closely tracks the national unemployment rate, which stood at 4.1% in October.

Although the labor market has remained resilient, Walsh pointed to several pressures on household finances, including wage growth lagging inflation, declining personal savings, and rising balances on credit cards, auto loans and student loans.

Borrowers who took out mortgages in recent years at higher interest rates may also face affordability challenges that make timely payments more difficult, Walsh remarked. Changes to mortgage relief programs over the past year, including the removal of some COVID-era flexibilities, could be adding to financial pressures for some homeowners.

#53172. Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1157 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am.
  • Industry observers note that the world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy.
  • A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am.

Industry observers note that the world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Sources indicate that sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

In a recent development, the window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

Recent findings suggest that competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”.

The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each upcoming model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

In a recent development, momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

In a recent development, learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Sources indicate that iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

Industry observers note that jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

At AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”.

Finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook says Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”.

Prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”.

Swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Farecast, the airfare prediction organization I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

Recent findings suggest that A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments manufacturer whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, said it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”.

Recent findings suggest that so pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one major shot once you have it.

Industry observers note that chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

Sources indicate that to repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one notes, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

Recent findings suggest that in AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (833 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • According to recent reports, the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

According to recent reports, the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

In a recent development, “Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

Industry observers note that “The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

Sources indicate that the terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

Sources indicate that “Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan remarked in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an crucial step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Recent findings suggest that inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

In a recent development, “I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel mentioned. “I think it’s vital to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker remarked workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

In a recent development, “A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really key component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

Why Compass wants the MLS antitrust dispute out of Fresh York

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (872 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Compass International Holdings and a group of seven MLS plaintiffs are asking a federal judge in Newly introduced York to decide if and where their antitrust battle over MLS cooperation and listing submission rules should proceed.
  • 13 letter, Compass mentioned it will seek to dismiss a consolidated declaratory judgment action filed by seven multiple listing services headquartered in Arizona, California, Colorado and North Carolina, or, alternatively, to sever and transfer each MLS’s claims to the district where Compass has brought its own antitrust case against that MLS.
  • The lawsuit was filed in the Southern District of Latest York (SDNY) by Arizona Regional MLS (ARMLS), OneKey MLS, MLSListings, Bridge MLS, Canopy MLS, Recolorado, Hive MLS and Doorify MLS after Compass sent letters to MLSs across the country in September demanding that they stop fining agents for publicly marketing office exclusive listings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Compass International Holdings and a group of seven MLS plaintiffs are asking a federal judge in Newly introduced York to decide if and where their antitrust battle over MLS cooperation and listing submission rules should proceed. The parties filed dueling letters earlier this month laying out competing narratives on forum shopping, efficiency and control over nationwide litigation.

Sources indicate that in a Nov. 13 letter, Compass mentioned it will seek to dismiss a consolidated declaratory judgment action filed by seven multiple listing services headquartered in Arizona, California, Colorado and North Carolina, or, alternatively, to sever and transfer each MLS’s claims to the district where Compass has brought its own antitrust case against that MLS.

The lawsuit was filed in the Southern District of Latest York (SDNY) by Arizona Regional MLS (ARMLS), OneKey MLS, MLSListings, Bridge MLS, Canopy MLS, Recolorado, Hive MLS and Doorify MLS after Compass sent letters to MLSs across the country in September demanding that they stop fining agents for publicly marketing office exclusive listings.

The MLSs are seeking declarations that their rules comply with Section 1 of the Sherman Act and state antitrust statutes, and an injunction preventing Compass from “bringing or pursuing any claim” against them over those rules, according to the amended complaint.

According to recent reports, compass told the court the MLSs’ consolidated suit is an “improper anticipatory filing” under the Declaratory Judgment Act. Citing prior legal precedent, Compass argued that courts may decline jurisdiction when declaratory relief is used “for procedural fencing.” The manufacturer pointed to its September demand letters, the sue‑by deadlines it set, and a series of deadline extensions it granted as part of what it characterizes as a good‑faith attempt to resolve the dispute short of litigation.

According to recent reports, in the letter, Compass noted counsel for ARMLS, Doorify MLS and Hive MLS requested a draft release and then sought additional time, citing illness and scheduling constraints, before filing this lawsuit in Upcoming York without substantively responding to the demands. Other MLSs, including MLSListings, BridgeMLS, REcolorado and Canopy MLS, also requested extensions to respond to the demand letter, Compass said.

It has been revealed that compass alleges the MLSs used those extensions to prepare the SDNY filing and then sued the day after certain extended deadlines expired. Compass also emphasized that it has since filed “home‑district” actions against each MLS in its own federal district, along with additional suits against other MLSs.

Since those damages claims cannot be resolved by declaratory relief alone and involve additional parties and provisions, Compass argued in its letter that the SDNY case would not “settle the controversy.”.

However, as an alternative to dismissal, Compass is asking the court to sever each MLS’s claims and transfer them to the districts where the company’s separate antitrust suits are pending: Arizona, Northern California, Colorado and the Western and Eastern Districts of North Carolina.

It has been revealed that compass said the MLSs themselves allege they act “independently,” operate in distinct regional markets, have different governing boards and maintain non‑identical rules. Having a shared adversary in Compass and a similar form demand letter do not make their policies a single transaction or occurrence, the firm told the court.

In a response letter sent on Wednesday, counsel for the MLS plaintiffs urged the court to keep the case and deny Compass’s anticipated motions. The MLSs argue that the SDNY suit is a textbook use of the Declaratory Judgment Act and that Compass, from its Newly introduced York headquarters, orchestrated a “nationwide campaign” against cooperation rules that should be resolved in a single forum.

The MLSs characterize Compass’s pre‑suit communications differently, saying the firm presented only two options: abandon their cooperation rules entirely in exchange for what they describe as a “toothless” release that left them under a “perpetual threat” of future litigation, or face antitrust lawsuits without clarity as to timing or venue.

The MLSs also dispute Compass’s forum‑shopping argument, emphasizing that they sued the brokerage in its home district and in the same court where Compass chose to litigate a separate cooperation‑rule case against Zillow.

By contrast, they say Compass’s 15-case strategy across 11 districts invites inconsistent outcomes and “massive inefficiencies.”.

Recent findings suggest that the MLS plaintiffs also pushed back on Compass’s bid to sever and transfer their claims. They argue their joinder meets federal procedure rules because each MLS plaintiff faces the same type of challenge from a single defendant over listing-submission rules that, while not identical, share common structure and legal challenges.

Recent findings suggest that regarding the possibility of transferring the case, the MLSs say Compass cannot meet its burden to show, by clear and convincing evidence, that moving the case would serve the convenience of parties and witnesses and the interests of justice. They feel that their choice of Compass’s home forum is entitled to substantial deference, particularly because Compass’s executives and documents are in Fresh York.

According to recent reports, it remains to be seen how the court will rule on this concern. However, the ruling will help determine where and how promptly federal courts address the legality of MLS rules that require brokers to share publicly marketed listings with other brokers through the cooperative database of the MLS.

  • 17: ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am.

Patch, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA stated Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Patch, Tuesday Nov. 17: ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff. Read our follow-up story for details. This story has been updated with ULA’s preliminary findings.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit Sunday, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle tech giant’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased.

ULA said Sunday that it didn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it would work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as rapidly as possible.

Amazon Leo remarked in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term looks for Vulcan.”.

According to recent reports, the rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to reach orbit. The Centaur, powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris, appears to have started normally and couldn’t make up for the shortfall. ULA appears to have lost telemetry and the mission about 10 minutes into the flight.

Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t said what caused the shortfall.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had introduced 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Sources indicate that melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 introduces reserved on Blue Origin’s Latest Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

It has been revealed that amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security introduces after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the Latest Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported.

Recent findings suggest that ULA is also under newly introduced leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

Broker Action Coalition pushes for QM change on compensation cap

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Broker Action Coalition (BAC) is proposing a change to federal mortgage rules that would exclude lender-paid mortgage broker compensation from the Qualified Mortgage (QM) points-and-fees calculation, aligning its treatment with compensation paid to retail lenders’ employee loan officers.
  • In a white paper recently released by BAC, the coalition argues that the current rules create an uneven playing field between independent mortgage brokers and retail lenders, particularly on smaller-balance loans.
  • Under the Ability-to-Repay/Qualified Mortgage rule, points and fees generally cannot exceed 3% of a loan amount for loans of $137,958 or more in 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Broker Action Coalition (BAC) is proposing a change to federal mortgage rules that would exclude lender-paid mortgage broker compensation from the Qualified Mortgage (QM) points-and-fees calculation, aligning its treatment with compensation paid to retail lenders’ employee loan officers.

In a white paper recently released by BAC, the coalition argues that the current rules create an uneven playing field between independent mortgage brokers and retail lenders, particularly on smaller-balance loans.

Under the Ability-to-Repay/Qualified Mortgage rule, points and fees generally cannot exceed 3% of a loan amount for loans of $137,958 or more in 2026. Smaller loans are subject to graduated percentage and dollar limits.

Right now, compensation paid by a wholesale lender to an independent mortgage broker counts toward that limit, while compensation paid by a retail lender to its own employee loan officer is excluded.

Sources indicate that the coalition argues that both types of compensation are often funded through the interest rate and are indistinguishable from the borrower’s perspective. The difference can leave brokers with less room to cover other fees that count toward the cap, potentially causing otherwise qualifying loans to exceed the limit while losing QM status and its associated liability protections.

The disparity is particularly pronounced on smaller loans, where the dollar limits leave less room for additional charges. The coalition noted small-balance and rural loans are particularly vulnerable because fixed-dollar charges consume a larger share of the available cap.

The white paper also points to a decline in small-dollar mortgage lending. The share of home purchase loans under $70,000 fell from more than 11% in 2011 to less than 4% in 2020, citing research from Pew Charitable Trusts, the Urban Institute and the Department of Housing and Urban Development.

In rural and lower-cost markets, the group argues, the restrictions can make it harder for brokers to compete for loans that are already less financially attractive to originate.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau‘s 2013 rulemaking established the distinction between employee and broker compensation. At the time, the bureau remarked including broker compensation in the calculation could help reduce the risk of mortgage brokers steering borrowers toward more expensive transactions.

The coalition acknowledges that consumer protection concern but argues that subsequent regulations addressing loan originator compensation and steering have made the points-and-fees restriction a less targeted way to address the issue.

Specifically, the group points to existing rules that prohibit loan originator compensation from varying based on a loan’s interest rate or other terms, as well as a separate prohibition on steering borrowers toward transactions that provide greater compensation.

The proposed reform would take two approaches: The primary proposal is a statutory amendment to the Truth in Lending Act that would exclude rate-funded creditor-to-broker compensation from the points-and-fees definition when it is paid under a compliant loan originator compensation agreement.

The parallel regulatory proposal would ask the CFPB to amend Regulation Z to create the same exclusion.

In a recent development, “The proposed reform would remove an inequitable regulatory constraint without changing the competitive forces that influence compensation today,” the paper reads. “While individual brokerages may adjust their compensation arrangements, there is little evidence to suggest that the reform would materially diminish the wholesale channel‘s overall pricing competitiveness.”.

Under the proposed language, the exclusion would apply only when compensation is funded through the interest rate, is not paid directly by the borrower or financed into the loan amount, and is established through a standing agreement between the creditor and broker that does not vary based on individual loan terms.

It has been revealed that the coalition remarked the proposed requirements would prevent brokers from adjusting compensation on individual loans to circumvent the cap. The change would leave the 3% limit and existing compensation and anti-steering rules intact, with borrower-paid compensation and other fees still subject to the cap.

It has been revealed that data from two wholesale lenders representing $13.4 billion in combined 2026 production showed that loans with 2.75% broker compensation accounted for 14.53% of units and 12.41% of volume. BAC said the figures indicate most brokered loans close with lower compensation.

Recent findings suggest that the group also argued that the CFPB has authority under the Truth in Lending Act to make the change to preserve access to affordable mortgage credit. It cited the bureau’s 2019 assessment of the Ability-to-Repay and Qualified Mortgage rule, which documented fee waivers and other challenges affecting smaller brokered loans.

Industry observers note that nvidia, IBM and Fermilab announced new tools for quantum error correction on Nov. 16, and the news comes amid a debate in the crypto industry about "Q-Day," the moment when a quantum computer will be able to break Bitcoin's cryptography. As of Monday, the price of Bitcoin stands at $64,580.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia released a newly introduced decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, on Nov. 16. According to the company, the algorithm delivers up to 13,000x faster decoding compared with existing leading algorithms, and it cuts the computation time for researching new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to 45 minutes.

Nvidia mentioned that the algorithm helps researchers find designs that use physical qubits more efficiently, "shortening the path to practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.".

Sources indicate that nvidia and IBM also announced prepares for a modular quantum computing codesign platform with Fermilab. IBM and Nvidia are placing Nvidia DGX B200 systems next to IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, and researchers will use the platform to develop and test error-correction codes.

"Making quantum computers useful for science requires advances in error correction, applications and the systems that bring quantum processors and accelerated computing together," said Krysta Svore, vice president of applied research for quantum computing at Nvidia.

A 2022 study by researchers from the University of Sussex estimated that breaking Bitcoin's encryption within a day would require around 13 million physical qubits.

IBM Quantum Nighthawk, which IBM calls its fastest quantum processor, has 120 qubits. According to Nvidia, errors in quantum processors "limit the complexity and duration of the computations they can perform.".

In 2024, Bitcoin developer Hunter Beast proposed BIP-360, a new output type that would protect coins from quantum attacks. In July 2025, Casa co-founder Jameson Lopp also suggested a plan to phase out legacy signatures and move coins to quantum-resistant addresses.

Early coins mined by Satoshi Nakamoto sit on addresses with public keys that are already visible on the blockchain.

In November 2024, NIST proposed to stop allowing vulnerable public-key algorithms, including elliptic curve cryptography, after 2035.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:17 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Recent findings suggest that financial software company Intuit Inc. today revealed that it has agreed to sell its Mailchimp email marketing business to Italian technology holding company Bending Spoons S.p.A. for about $3.68 billion.

In a recent development, coming five years after Intuit agreed to acquire Mailchimp for $12 billion, the sale price is less than a third of what the company paid. The 2021 purchase was the largest in Intuit’s history at the time.

According to recent reports, although Bending Spoons describes the transaction as all-cash, Intuit will reinvest $368 million of its proceeds in newly issued Bending Spoons shares. That leaves Intuit with $3.31 billion in cash from the sale, according to the companies. Included in the deal is The Rocket Science Group LLC, the legal entity behind Mailchimp. Closing is expected in early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals.

Selling Mailchimp is noted to sharpen Intuit’s focus on the artificial intelligence-native tools it has built to help businesses win latest customers, manage their pipeline and grow. Once the deal closes, Intuit intends to use the cash proceeds to buy back its own shares before the end of fiscal 2027.

Jack Tam, a senior vice president at Intuit, stated the firm is confident Bending Spoons “will lead Mailchimp to continued success in this next chapter.”.

Growth at Mailchimp has stalled in recent quarters. Revenue from the business fell 1% to $313 million in the quarter ended Oct. 31. Intuit’s full-year guidance has Mailchimp revenue coming in flat to down 1%. In November 2024, Chief Financial Officer Sandeep Aujla told analysts that Intuit was seeing higher churn from smaller Mailchimp customers.

“Mailchimp is a powerful brand, built over two decades of reshaping the email marketing category and redefining how companies grow their audiences,” said Luca Ferrari, co-founder and chief executive of Bending Spoons. “We’re honored to welcome it to Bending Spoons and excited about what we can accomplish together.”.

Ferrari added that Bending Spoons aims to invest substantially in Mailchimp after closing. According to Bending Spoons, the transformation of a business it acquires is typically deep, entailing reorganized teams, overhauled technology and redesigned user interfaces.

Industry observers note that founded in 2013, Bending Spoons has built a portfolio of digital businesses that includes AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Tractive, Vimeo and WeTransfer. Since listing on the Nasdaq in July, the company has also completed acquisitions of Airtable Inc. for $1.285 billion and whiteboard platform Miro for $1.355 billion.

Sources indicate that intuit announced the sale alongside its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results. For the quarter, it reported adjusted earnings per share of $2.91, up 56% from $1.87 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $4.35 billion, up 12% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting adjusted earnings of $2.70 per share on revenue of $4.31 billion.

Sources indicate that for its fiscal second quarter, Intuit expects adjusted earnings per share of $3.17 to $3.22 on revenue of $4.93 billion to $4.95 billion. Intuit lowered its full-year revenue guidance to between $23.08 billion and $23.37 billion.

Behind the cut is Credit Karma, the manufacturer’s personal finance and credit score service, which is now forecast to grow 3% to 7% this fiscal year, down from 11% to 13% previously. Intuit reiterated its full-year adjusted earnings guidance of $22.88 to $23.12 per share. None of the guidance includes the effect of the Mailchimp sale.

Intuit shares fell more than 10% in after-hours trading.

#53159. Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am.
  • It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows firm,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows.
  • These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a upcoming OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am.

It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows firm,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a upcoming OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”.

Instead, the Copilot as “a upcoming OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

Industry observers note that microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

The high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

Operating systems like Windows provide consumers with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the newly introduced Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

Industry observers note that the Newly introduced OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

In a recent development, presently, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the newly introduced Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as Upcoming OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

Sources indicate that if you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, consumers don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

Recent findings suggest that “We increasingly think of all our apps together as a latest operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” mentioned Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

Recent findings suggest that the end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella mentioned.

The Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.
