#53158. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1515 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1515 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.
  • Sources indicate that ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Sources indicate that ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He mentioned he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

It has been revealed that “I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan remarked. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he remarked. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

Recent findings suggest that agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Industry observers note that sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

According to recent reports, daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

According to recent reports, “By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and fresh construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

Recent findings suggest that “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova stated. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Sources indicate that andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

Recent findings suggest that she leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

It has been revealed that hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

Industry observers note that he also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

It has been revealed that “In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer remarked. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

Recent findings suggest that she played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea indicates she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, Latest Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share latest songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he remarked. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

Industry observers note that on setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

Sources indicate that as for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova mentioned she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

In a recent development, so the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova remarked, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Matt Jones’ nomination to serve as assistant secretary for housing at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and as Federal Housing Administration (FHA) commissioner advanced in the Senate on Thursday, moving through committee on a narrow vote.
  • The Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs approved his nomination 13-11, sending it to the full Senate for consideration.
  • In a recent development, committee chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) stated Jones’ mix of public- and private-sector experience is central to his support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Matt Jones’ nomination to serve as assistant secretary for housing at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and as Federal Housing Administration (FHA) commissioner advanced in the Senate on Thursday, moving through committee on a narrow vote.

The Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs approved his nomination 13-11, sending it to the full Senate for consideration. Jones would permanently fill the vacancy left by Frank Cassidy in June and succeed Joseph Gormley, who has been serving in the role on an acting basis.

In a recent development, committee chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) stated Jones’ mix of public- and private-sector experience is central to his support. According to Scott, housing affordability remains one of the biggest challenges facing families across America, but if confirmed, Jones “will play an notable role in implementing the 21st Century Road to Housing Act and helping more families achieve the American dream of home ownership.”.

Jones currently serves as HUD’s deputy assistant secretary for single-family housing. He previously was associate vice president of government housing finance at the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), senior adviser for capital markets at Amerifirst Home Mortgage, and senior counsel for the Senate’s Finance and Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs committees.The 13-11 vote reflected partisan divisions over the direction of federal housing policy and FHA’s role in addressing affordability and ownership gaps.

Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the committee’s ranking member, voted against the nomination, saying Jones’ office has “cut resources for first-time homebuyers and proposed weak rules for keeping foreclosed homes in the hands of families instead of corporations.”.

Sources indicate that “We should vote to make life more affordable for American families. But these nominees will do the opposite, accelerating the Trump administration‘s disastrous economic policies,” Warren stated. If confirmed, Jones would oversee FHA’s single-family, multifamily and health care mortgage insurance portfolios. FHA at the moment insures roughly $2 trillion in mortgages.

The FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund posted a strong financial performance in fiscal year 2026, even as its capital ratio declined from 2025 levels. The results have renewed industry pressure on FHA to cut annual mortgage insurance premiums to ease costs for first-time and lower-income borrowers.

Jones would also inherit an agency that has seen a series of policy adjustments under HUD Secretary Scott Turner, including efforts to revise servicing standards and modernize technology infrastructure.

MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit said the trade group supports the nomination due to Jones’ “extensive mortgage industry experience, deep understanding of government housing finance, and leadership of FHA’s single-family operations.”.

“We urge the full Senate to confirm Matt Jones before the 119th Congress adjourns and look forward to working with him and HUD to continue modernizing FHA programs and to improve affordability for owning and renting a home,” Broeksmit noted.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elite university Harvard maintains significant Bitcoin exposure as it holds over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin ETF, a recent regulatory filing has revealed.

Harvard University remains highly exposed to Bitcoin (BTC) as the elite institution continues to hold over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF).

As per Bitcoin Magazine’s Nov. 16 report, Harvard Management Company, which manages Harvard University’s endowment, held 3,044,612 shares of BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) as of Sept. 30, 2026.

It has been revealed that the Form 13F filing by Harvard University with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) demonstrated that its investment in the Bitcoin ETF was worth roughly $144.1 million at the end of the third quarter.

Recent findings suggest that notably, Harvard did not change its Bitcoin ETF share count during the third quarter. The university held the same number of shares as reported at the end of June.

Harvard first disclosed its investment in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF during the second quarter of 2025.

As per Harvard's Form 13F filing submitted on Aug. 8, 2025, it held 1,906,000 IBIT shares at the end of the second quarter. The investment was worth roughly $116.7 million as of June 30.

The university subsequently increased its Bitcoin exposure significantly.

For instance, at the end of September 2025, Harvard held 6,813,612 IBIT shares, worth roughly $442.9 million. The Bitcoin ETF was the biggest investment that Harvard publicly reported at the time.

In a recent development, later, however, the university started trimming its Bitcoin exposure. For example, during the fourth quarter of 2025, Harvard reduced its IBIT holdings by about 21.4%. Its total share holdings fell to 5.35 million.

During the first quarter of 2026, Harvard again reduced its Bitcoin exposure by 43.1%. This brought down the number of IBIT shares to roughly 3.04 million.

Since then, the university has maintained this number of shares. Harvard's quarter-end share count has remained unchanged in recent quarters.

Harvard University is not the only top-tier American university that has gained exposure to the biggest cryptocurrency by market capitalization.

In October 2024, Emory University became the first U.S. university endowment to publicly disclose its holdings in a Bitcoin ETF.

It held roughly 2.7 million shares of Grayscale’s Bitcoin Mini Trust, worth over $15 million at the time.

Meanwhile, in May 2025, Brown University disclosed its holdings of 105,000 shares of BlackRock's IBIT, worth roughly $4.9 million as of March 31 of that year.

Later, Brown doubled its stake, bringing its holdings to 212,500 shares.

Meanwhile, Dartmouth College has also joined the list of universities with exposure to cryptocurrency ETFs.

Recent findings suggest that in its recent filing, Dartmouth College disclosed that it held 201,531 IBIT shares. The investment was worth roughly $9.5 million as of the end of September 2026.

#53155. Tech Report: What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

Tech Report: What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am.
  • Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.
  • That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am.

Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.

That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.

According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.”.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft says active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the tech giant posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began.

The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services.

According to recent reports, microsoft hasn’t said what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report.

Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze.

Sources indicate that that’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it.

Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report.

In a recent development, when traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage.

Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny:.

According to recent reports, microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load.

The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report.

In a recent development, the company certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure.

Recent findings suggest that the safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold. Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate glitch,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global.

The gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption.

Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the company put it, so email stayed down.

It has been revealed that microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t quickly undo one that was months old.

Industry observers note that the company’s systems automatically shifted traffic from unresponsive servers to healthy ones, and the extra load triggered the same bug on those servers, too. About 10 hours in, engineers turned off some of that automatic rerouting.

Sources indicate that charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posted an abridged version of the report on X late Sunday. “We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” he wrote.

Lamanna had previewed the findings Friday afternoon, blaming “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” for the slow recovery, as GeekWire reported when Microsoft declared the outage over.

Sources indicate that microsoft notes it has rolled back the defective code, added server capacity and monitoring, and put new limits on how traffic is redistributed to avoid another cascade. A final report with a full list of repairs is due Nov. 20.

Recent findings suggest that it may also answer the biggest question the preliminary report leaves open: why the walls between regions didn’t stop the outage from spreading worldwide. Microsoft blames that on “a separate problem,” apart from the July bug, but hasn’t remarked what it was.

John Forsyth, Cirrus Logic President and CEO, Elected Chair of Semiconductor Industry Association

💡 Key Takeaways

  • "Congratulations to John Forsyth on his election as SIA Chair.
  • Forsyth brings more than 20 years of experience in semiconductor industry leadership.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SAN JOSE, Calif., Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) today announced that Cirrus Logic (NASDAQ: CRUS) President and CEO John Forsyth has been elected Chair of the SIA Board of Directors. Tom Caulfield, Executive Chairman of GlobalFoundries (NASDAQ: GFS), was elected Vice Chair. AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) Chair and CEO Lisa Su, who served as 2026 Chair, will continue to serve on the Board and the Leadership Committee. SIA, the voice of the semiconductor industry, represents 99% of the U.S. semiconductor industry by revenue and nearly two-thirds of non-U.S. chip firms.

"Congratulations to John Forsyth on his election as SIA Chair. John has been a trusted partner since my first day at SIA, and he brings steady, strategic judgment to a pivotal year for our industry," said SIA President and CEO Michael Robbins. "With a newly introduced Congress, SIA's 50th anniversary, and the work of extending the Advanced Manufacturing Investment Credit ahead of us, I look forward to working with John, Tom Caulfield, and our entire Board to strengthen America's semiconductor leadership. I also want to thank Lisa Su for an outstanding year as our Chair. Her steadfast leadership strengthens SIA and our industry, and I am tremendously grateful for her guidance and counsel.".

Forsyth brings more than 20 years of experience in semiconductor industry leadership. As president and CEO of Cirrus Logic, he leads the organization in developing high-precision, low-power audio and mixed-signal semiconductor solutions for a broad range of consumer, automotive, and industrial applications. Forsyth has served as president and chief executive officer of Cirrus Logic since January 2021. He joined the company in 2014 through its acquisition of Wolfson Microelectronics and was named president in 2020 after previous roles including chief strategy officer and vice president of marketing.

"I'm honored to serve as SIA Chair at such an important time for our industry," said John Forsyth, president and CEO of Cirrus Logic. "America's leadership in the next wave of semiconductor innovation depends on both a thriving domestic industry and close collaboration between that industry and government. I look forward to working with SIA's Board of Directors and members to strengthen that collaboration, accelerate the build-out of a more resilient domestic supply chain, and keep the U.S. at the forefront of this critical technology.".

Industry observers note that about SIAThe Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) is the voice of the semiconductor industry, one of America's top export industries and a key driver of America's economic strength, national security, and global competitiveness. SIA represents 99% of the U.S. semiconductor industry by revenue and nearly two-thirds of non-U.S. chip firms. Through this coalition, SIA seeks to strengthen leadership of semiconductor manufacturing, design, and research by working with Congress, the Administration, and key industry stakeholders around the world to encourage policies that fuel innovation, propel business, and drive international competition. Learn more at semiconductors.org.
